en: The Lineage of Buddhas 2:
The Story of Sumedha’s Aspiration “For a hundred thousand aeons...”
And four more incalculable [aeons];
there was a city named Amara,
beautiful to behold and delightful to the mind.
Not devoid of the ten sounds,
provided with food and drink,
the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, and so forth.
With drums, conchs, and chariots;
eat and drink indeed,
for it is proclaimed with food and drink.
A city complete in all its parts,
where every function is fulfilled,
and endowed with the seven treasures.
Crowded with various people,
it was like a prosperous city of the gods—
a dwelling for those who perform meritorious deeds.
In the city of Amarāvatī,
there was a brahmin named Sumedha,
who had accumulated many tens of millions of wealth.
Possessing abundant wealth and grain,
a reciter who has mastered the mantras,
one who has gone to the further shore of the three Vedas.
Having reached perfection in the marks, in history, and in his own Dhamma,
he sat down in seclusion.
I thought thus at that time:
"Rebirth is indeed suffering,
as is the dissolution of the body."
Subject to birth, subject to aging,
and subject to sickness at that time;
[seeking] the ageless, deathless, and secure.
I shall seek out Nibbāna.
What if I were now [to examine] this putrid body,
filled with various kinds of filth?
Having abandoned it, I shall go,
indifferent and without desire;
that path will indeed exist.
It is not impossible that it cannot be attained;
I shall seek that path for the sake of liberation from existence.
Just as when suffering exists,
that which is called happiness also exists;
so too, while existence exists, [non-existence exists].
Even non-existence (vibhava) is to be desired.
Just as when heat exists,
something else that is cool exists;
Thus, while these three kinds of fire exist,
Nibbāna is what should be sought;
just as when evils exist, [the good must be sought].
Even the auspicious exists;
even so, while birth exists,
the unborn is to be sought.
Just as a man who has fallen into excrement,
upon seeing a full pond,
does not seek out that pond.
That is no fault of the pond.
So too, while the pond of the Deathless exists,
there is merely the defilement of impurity.
He does not search for that pond;
there is no fault in the pond of the Deathless.
Just as one besieged by enemies—
While there is still a path for going,
that man does not flee;
it is no fault of the straight way.
Thus obstructed by defilements,
though the auspicious path exists,
he does not seek that way.
There is no fault in the path to peace.
Just as a sick man,
while a physician is available, [remains ill]...
If one does not have that disease treated,
the fault does not lie with the physician.
In the same way, regarding the diseases of the defilements...
Afflicted and oppressed,
he does not seek out that teacher;
this is no fault of the leader.
Just as a person, loathing a corpse tied around his neck,
would set it free and go away;
Happy, at ease, and self-mastered.
Even so is this putrid body,
a heap of various corpses.
Having cast it away, I would go on,
indifferent and without desire,
just as one leaves a place of excrement.
Having discarded dung, men and women depart,
indifferent and having no further need for it.
In the same way, having cast aside this body filled with various kinds of filth, I shall depart.
Just as one might build a hut after evacuating its dung,
or just as one might repair an old, leaking boat that is taking on water.
They depart, having abandoned the master,
indifferent and without desire;
even so do I [regard] this body.
With nine holes leaking constantly,
I shall abandon it and depart,
just as owners leave a worn-out boat.
Just as a man traveling with thieves, taking their goods,
might see the danger of having those goods seized, and—
Having abandoned it, he goes away.
In this very way, this body is like a great thief.
"Having abandoned this, I shall go away out of fear for the destruction of my wholesome states.
Having thought thus, I—
Having given hundreds of millions of wealth to those who had protectors and those who were protectorless,
I went to the Himalayas.
Not far from the Himalayas is a mountain named Dhammika;
there my well-constructed hermitage stands.
A leaf-hut was well-constructed.
There I built a walking-path,
free from the five defects.
Endowed with the eight qualities,
I acquired the power of direct knowledge;
there, I cast off my garment.
I wore a garment of bark that had reached nine defects,
yet possessed twelve virtues.
Abandoning the leaf-hut, which was beset by eight defects,
I approached the foot of a tree.
Having reached tenfold excellence,
I abandoned the sown and planted grain without remainder.
I took ripe fruit endowed with manifold virtues; there,
I applied myself with supreme effort.
Sitting, standing, and walking,
within seven days I attained the power of direct knowledge.
Thus, when I had attained accomplishment and gained mastery in the Teaching,
the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara appeared.
The Leader of the World arose.
When he arises, when he is born,
when he awakens, and when he teaches the Dhamma;
Absorbed in the delight of jhāna, he did not perceive the four signs in that borderland region.
Having invited the Tathāgata,
they cleared the path for his arrival with joyful minds.
At that time,
having gone forth from Sakassama,
I was shaking off my garments of bark.
Then I went into the sky.
Seeing the people born of the Vedas,
joyful, delighted, and exultant;
Having descended from the sky,
he immediately questioned the people:
"Joyful, with uplifted hearts and delighted..."
“The great multitude has been born from the Vedas;
whose path is being cleared—
the straight way that leads to the goal?”
When questioned by me, they replied:
"The Jina named Dīpaṅkara, the unsurpassed Buddha in the world."
The Leader of the World has arisen;
his path is being cleared—
the straight way for traveling.
Having heard the Buddha’s own words,
joy arose at that very moment as he spoke, "Buddha! Buddha!"
I proclaimed my joy.
Standing there, with a mind both delighted and stirred by awe, I reflected.
‘Here I shall sow the seeds;
let not the opportune moment pass me by.
‘If you would clear it for the Buddha, [then do so].’
Grant me a single opportunity;
I too shall clear the straight path for traveling.”
They then gave me the opportunity to purify the straight path,
as I reflected, "Buddha, Buddha."
I was then clearing the path.
While my work was not yet finished,
the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara appeared.
With four hundred thousand [monks],
who possessed the six direct knowledges, were such-like,
had destroyed the taints, and were stainless.
The Victor proceeded along the direct path.
Processions came forth to meet him,
and many drums were sounded.
The humans and gods were delighted and raised shouts of "Well done!
The gods beheld the humans.
Both humans and deities,
with palms joined in reverence,
follow the Tathāgata.
The gods with celestial music and humans with human music—
both of them desisting from these, [they dwell in peace].
They follow the Tathāgata with celestial mandārava flowers,
lotuses, and pārichattaka trees.
The gods, having come from the sky, sprinkle divine sandalwood powder, scattering it all around.
And the gods, having gone into the intermediate space,
scatter pure, excellent perfumes in every direction.
Campaka, sarala, nīpa, nāga, punnāga, and ketaka—
these they toss up in every direction.
The men who had gone to the surface of the earth—
having loosened my hair there,
as well as my bark garment and my hide;
Having spread out upon the *kalala*,
I lay down face downwards.
“The Buddha, having stepped upon me, ...”
Let him go with his disciples; do not step upon the mud,
for it will be for my benefit.”
As I lay upon the ground,
such was the thought in my mind:
"If I so desired, today..."
May you burn away my defilements.
What need have I for living in disguise?
Here, let me realize the Dhamma.
Having attained omniscience,
I shall become a Buddha in this world with its devas.
What need have I for this single crossing?
By me, a man who perceives my strength;
having attained omniscience,
I shall ferry across the world together with its devas.
By this service rendered by me to the Supreme Person,
having attained omniscience,
I shall ferry across the vast multitude of people;
having cut off the stream of saṃsāra and shattered the three realms of existence.
Having boarded the ship of the Dhamma,
I shall ferry across the world together with its devas.
Human birth, the perfection of gender,
The cause is seeing the Teacher;
the going forth, the perfection of qualities,
the requisite conditions, and zeal.
‘Through the convergence of eight factors,
the aspiration succeeds.
Thus spoke Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World.
The recipient of the oblations,
standing at my head,
spoke these words:
“Behold this ascetic,
the matted-hair ascetic who practices fierce austerities;
for immeasurable eons...”
"A Buddha shall appear in the world.
Having gone forth from the delightful city called Kapila, the Tathāgata [attained enlightenment].
Having exerted himself in striving and performed ascetic practices,
at the foot of the Goatherd’s Tree,
Having sat down there, the Tathāgata,
taking up the milk-rice,
will proceed to the Nerañjarā River.
On the bank of the Nerañjarā,
that Conqueror ate the milk-rice by way of the specially prepared excellent path.
He will approach the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Then, having circumambulated it,
the Unsurpassed One will go to the seat of enlightenment.
At the foot of an assattha tree,
the one of great renown will awaken.
His mother, who gave him birth,
Her name shall be Māyā;
her father, named Suddhodana,
shall be this Gotama.
Free from taints, devoid of passion,
with peaceful minds and concentrated,
were Kolita and Upatissa.
The disciples shall be foremost;
he named Ānanda, as an attendant,
shall serve this Conqueror.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples;
they will be free from taints and devoid of passion.
With peaceful minds and concentrated,
they declare that the Bodhi of that Blessed One is the Assattha.
Citta and Hatthāḷavaka shall be the foremost attendants;
and Uttarā, the mother of Nanda, too.
"May they be foremost among those with bones.
Having heard these words of the Peerless Great Sage,
Men and gods were filled with joy,
exclaiming, "This, they say,
is the seed of a Buddha! And shouts of acclamation arose.
They clap their hands and laugh;
the ten thousand worlds, together with the devas, pay homage with palms joined.
"If we fail in the teaching of this Protector of the World,
in a future time..."
We shall stand face to face with him.
Just as people crossing a river might miss a ford;
Having taken hold at the lower ford,
he crosses over the great river;
even so do we all.
"If we release this Conqueror,
in a future time we shall stand face-to-face with him."
Dīpaṅkara, the knower of the world,
the receiver of offerings,
having proclaimed my deed, [said:]
I lifted my right foot.
Those sons of the Conqueror who were there circumambulated me.
The gods, humans, and asuras,
having paid homage, departed;
even as they were leaving my sight, [they continued on].
While the Leader of the World was with the Saṅgha,
I rose from my bed and then sat cross-legged.
I am happy through happiness,
delighted by rapture; I am suffused with joy.
I then assumed the cross-legged posture.
Having sat down cross-legged,
I then reflected thus:
“I have become a master in meditation;
I have reached perfection in the higher knowledges.
In this world of a thousand worlds, [I am the foremost].”
“There are no seers equal to me;
peerless among those possessing psychic powers,
I have obtained such happiness.”
As I sat cross-legged,
the ten thousand world-systems resounded with a great roar.
"You will certainly become a Buddha.
Those [signs] which appeared previously for Bodhisattvas when they sat upon the excellent throne;"
The signs appear;
they appear today.
The cold has departed.
The heat has subsided;
these signs are visible today—
surely you will become a Buddha.
The ten-thousandfold world system was silent and undisturbed;
today those very things are visible.
"You will certainly become a Buddha.
The great winds do not blow,
and the rivers do not flow."
Those flowers are visible today;
surely you will become a Buddha.
Flowers born on land and flowers born in water—
All of them blossom at that time;
today they have all blossomed—
surely you will become a Buddha.
Whether they be creepers or trees,
they all bear fruit today, laden with the weight of their fruit.
"You will certainly become a Buddha. For as long as these jewels,
both those dwelling in the sky and those dwelling on the earth,
continue to shine,"
These three jewels shine here;
you will certainly become a Buddha.
Both human and divine—
The four [brahmavihāras] are being practiced;
they resound on all sides:
"Surely you will become a Buddha."
The sky rains down various flowers even now;
they too are raining down today.
"You will certainly become a Buddha.
The great ocean heaves,
and the ten-thousandfold world system trembles."
They rejoice exceedingly, "Surely you will become a Buddha.
Even in the ten thousand hells, they cry out: "He will surely become a Buddha!"
The fires were extinguished at that very moment;
those fires are now extinguished,
so you will certainly become a Buddha.
The sun is clear,
and all the stars are visible;
even those are seen today.
"You will certainly become a Buddha.
At that time, water rose up from the earth even without being rained down.
The earth trembles and bursts asunder;
surely you will become a Buddha.
The hosts of stars shine forth.
Among the constellations in the circle of the sky,
when the moon is joined with Viśākhā,
you will certainly become a Buddha.
Those who used to emerge from their own dwellings— whether mountain caves or forest glens—
are today abandoned by those very dwellings.
"You will certainly become a Buddha.
For beings do not remain discontented for long;
they soon become satisfied."
If all these are satisfied today,
you will certainly become a Buddha;
your diseases will then be pacified.
And hunger shall perish;
these signs appear today—
surely you will become a Buddha.
Then lust becomes thin,
hatred and delusion perish;
all three have now vanished.
"You will certainly become a Buddha.
At that time there was no fear;
even today this is clearly seen.
By this sign we know for certain that you will become a Buddha;
the dust rising upward is being blown away.
Even today this is visible;
by this sign we know that you will certainly become a Buddha.
The foul odor departs,
and a divine fragrance wafts forth;
today that fragrance blows.
"You will certainly become a Buddha.
All the gods are visible,
with the exception of those who are formless."
All these are seen today;
surely you will become a Buddha.
As many as there are places called hells...
All were visible at that time;
today all these are visible—
surely you will become a Buddha.
At that time, walls, doors, and rocks did not act as obstructions;
they became like space.
"You will certainly become a Buddha.
At that moment, neither death nor rebirth exists."
These signs are now appearing;
you will certainly become a Buddha.
Exert firm energy!
"Do not turn back, go forward!
We too shall know this:
you will surely become a Buddha."
Having heard the Buddha’s word,
both the ten-thousandfold world system was thrilled, elated, and overjoyed.
I thought thus at that time:
"The Buddhas speak without duplicity;
the Jinas' words are never in vain."
There is no falsehood for the Buddhas;
"I shall certainly become a Buddha," just like a clod of earth thrown into the sky.
Surely it falls upon the ground;
even so, the word of the Best of Buddhas is certain and eternal.
There is nothing false about the Buddhas;
"I shall certainly become a Buddha," [he thought],
just as [it is certain] for all beings.
Death is constant and eternal;
likewise, the word of the Supreme Buddhas is constant and eternal.
There is nothing false about the Buddhas;
it is certain that I shall become a Buddha.
Just as when the night has come to an end...
The rising of the sun is certain;
likewise, the word of the Best of Buddhas is certain and eternal.
There is no falsehood in the Buddhas;
"I shall certainly become a Buddha"—
just as for one who has arisen from his bed.
The roar of the lion is constant;
likewise, the word of the supreme Buddhas is constant and eternal.
There is nothing false about the Buddhas;
it is certain that I shall become a Buddha,
just as [it is for] those who have conceived the thought of enlightenment.
The laying down of the burden is certain;
likewise, the word of the Supreme Buddhas is eternally enduring.
There is nothing false about the Buddhas;
it is certain that I shall become a Buddha.
Come now, [I shall cultivate] the qualities that make one a Buddha.
I investigate here and there—
above, below, and in the ten directions—
to the full extent of the element of phenomena.
Searching then, he beheld the first perfection of giving,
practiced by the great seers of old.
The great path practiced by the Buddhas of the past: "First,
you must firmly undertake this."
Go to the perfection of generosity if you wish to attain awakening;
just as a jar that is completely full, [so too is one who has perfected giving].
For whomever it may be who has lowered [the vessel],
the water vomits out entirely;
he does not preserve anything there.
In the same way, seeing beggars—
whether low, high, or middling—
give them gifts without exception.
Like a jar turned upside down.
These are not all there are of the Buddha-qualities that will come to be.
"I shall investigate other things as well,
those qualities that ripen enlightenment.
While investigating, I then beheld—
The second is the perfection of virtue;
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this second one,
go forth to the perfection of virtue.”
If you wish to attain enlightenment,
just as a yak, when its tail has become entangled in something;
There one meets death,
yet does not lose its tail; even so,
you [should act] toward the four stages.
Fulfill the precepts;
protect your virtue at all times,
as the yak protects its tail.
The qualities of a Buddha will not be merely these many;
I shall seek out others as well.
"Those qualities that ripen enlightenment"—
searching then, I saw the third perfection, renunciation.
Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old—
first, you [should practice] this third [foundation of mindfulness].
Having firmly undertaken them,
go to the perfection of renunciation,
if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as a man who has lived long in a prison and is suffering there does not conceive passion for it, so too...
He seeks only liberation.
In the same way, you should regard all states of existence as if they were a prison-house of filth.
Be intent upon renunciation for the sake of liberation from existence;
for these [fetters] are not merely so many.
The qualities of a Buddha shall come to be;
I shall also seek out those other qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
Searching then, I beheld the fourth perfection of wisdom,
practiced by the great seers of old.
Cultivated and repeatedly practiced.
“First, you must firmly undertake this fourth [duty],” he said.
Go to the perfection of wisdom if you wish to attain enlightenment,
just as a monk goes about seeking alms.
Whether low, high, or middling—
by not avoiding families in this way,
one obtains the means of subsistence.
In that same way, at all times,
by constantly questioning wise people,
you shall reach the perfection of wisdom.
You will attain full enlightenment.
For these qualities of a Buddha will not be merely so many; they shall be far more than this.
"I shall investigate other things as well,
those qualities that ripen enlightenment.
While investigating, I then beheld—
The fifth is the perfection of energy,
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this fifth [perfection],
go forth to the perfection of energy.”
If you wish to attain enlightenment,
[be like] the lion, the king of beasts,
whether sitting, standing, or walking.
He is one whose vigor does not falter,
always with a mind of exertion;
even so should you [be] toward all states of existence.
Exert firm energy;
having reached the perfection of energy,
you will attain full enlightenment.
The qualities of a Buddha will not be limited to just these many;
I shall seek out others as well.
“Those qualities that ripen enlightenment”— searching then,
I beheld the sixth perfection, patience.
Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old—
first, you [should practice] this sixth [foundation of mindfulness].
Having undertaken them firmly,
with a mind free from doubt regarding them,
you will attain full enlightenment.
Just as the earth indeed endures the depositing of everything,
both the pure and the impure,
so too does the wise person endure all things.
One does not harbor resentment because of that.
In the same way, you too should be patient with both honor and dishonor from everyone.
Having reached the perfection of patience,
you will attain full enlightenment.
For these [perfections] are not merely so many.
The qualities of a Buddha will come to be;
I shall also seek out those other qualities that ripen into enlightenment.”
Then, while searching,
I beheld the seventh perfection of truth,
as practiced by the great seers of old.
Cultivated and practiced repeatedly:
“First, you must firmly undertake this seventh [precept],” he said.
In that regard, being one whose word is free from duplicity,
you will attain full enlightenment.
Just as with the medicinal herb named...
Acting as a balance for the world with its gods,
it does not deviate from its course during the change of seasons or the rainy season.
In the same way, you too must not deviate from the path of truths;
having reached the perfection of truth, [you shall attain the goal].
You will attain full enlightenment.
For these qualities of a Buddha will not remain merely at this level.
"I shall investigate other things as well,
those factors that ripen enlightenment.
While investigating, I then saw—
The eighth is the perfection of determination,
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this eighth [precept],
remain unshakable therein.”
you shall attain full enlightenment.
Just like a rocky mountain,
immovable and firmly established;
It does not shake in violent winds,
but remains in its own place; even so,
you too [should remain] in your resolve.
Be ever immovable;
having reached the perfection of determination,
you shall attain supreme enlightenment.
The Buddha-qualities will not be merely these many;
I shall seek others as well.
"Those qualities that ripen enlightenment"—
searching then, I beheld the ninth perfection,
that of loving-kindness.
Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old—
first of all, you [should practice] this ninth [jhāna].
Having undertaken it firmly,
be peerless in loving-kindness if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as water, indeed,
toward both good and evil people,
imparts its coolness equally.
It sweeps away the dust and impurity.
In the same way, you should cultivate equanimity toward both the beneficial and the harmful through loving-kindness.
Having reached the perfection of loving-kindness,
you will attain full enlightenment;
for these [perfections] are not merely so many.
There will be the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall also seek out those other qualities that bring enlightenment to fruition.”
Searching then, I beheld the tenth perfection, equanimity,
as practiced by the great seers of old.
Cultivated and repeatedly practiced.
“First, you must firmly undertake this tenth [precept] and observe it;”
Becoming firm as the earth,
you shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Just as that which is called the earth...
Whether filth or purity is cast down,
he regards both with equanimity,
free from aversion and attachment.
In the same way, always remain like a balance scale toward pleasure and pain;
having reached the perfection of equanimity, [abide therein].
You shall attain full enlightenment.
Only so many factors exist in the world that ripen for enlightenment.
"There is nothing else for that;
stand firm therein.
For one who comprehends these phenomena,"
At the moment of the characteristic of the natural essence,
the earth of the ten thousandfold world-system trembled through the majesty of the Dhamma.
The earth trembles and roars like a field of sugarcane being crushed,
like a wheel spinning with oil.
Thus did the earth tremble,
as far as the assembly was gathered at the Buddha’s meal distribution.
Trembling there,
she lies on the ground, fainting;
thousands of jars—
And many hundreds of jars were there,
crushed and mangled,
clashing against one another.
Agitated, terrified, and afraid,
with minds bewildered and distressed,
the great multitude gathered together.
They approached Dīpaṅkara [and asked]:
“What will come to pass for the world—
will it be auspicious or evil?”
"The whole world is afflicted;
dispel that, O Visionary One!
Then he instructed them.
Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, said:
“Be undisturbed; do not be afraid of this trembling of the earth.”
Today I have made this prediction:
"He will become a Buddha in the world";
he now thoroughly comprehends the Dhamma.
The ancient path practiced by the Victors—
by thoroughly comprehending that Dhamma,
one reaches the plane of a Buddha without remainder.
Therefore this earth,
together with its ten thousand worlds and its gods,
has trembled. Having heard the Buddha’s word,
My mind was then extinguished;
all of them, having approached me,
once again paid homage.
Having undertaken the qualities of a Buddha and made my mind firm,
I paid homage to Dīpaṅkara.
Then they rose from their seats.
Both the devas and humans offered divine and human flowers.
They scatter flowers as he rises from his seat,
and they announce his well-being.
Both gods and humans [said]:
"A great boon has been sought by you;
may you obtain it as you desire."
May all calamities be avoided;
may sorrow and disease perish;
may no obstacles arise for you.
Quickly touch upon supreme enlightenment,
just as flowering trees burst into bloom when the proper season arrives.
In that same way, O Great Hero,
you blossom with the wisdom of a Buddha,
just as all those who have attained perfect enlightenment do.
Fulfilling the ten perfections;
even so, O Great Hero,
fulfill the ten perfections.
Just as all those who were perfectly awakened awakened at the seat of enlightenment,
so too may you, O Great Hero.
Awaken to the enlightenment of the Conquerors,
just as all those who were perfectly awakened set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
In that same way, O Great Hero,
set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
like the moon on the night of the full moon.
The pure one shines;
even so, you, O Puṇṇamana,
shine throughout the ten thousandfold world-system.
Just as the sun, freed from Rāhu,
shines forth with its heat, even so,
having been released from the worlds, [the Tathāgata shines].
You shine with glory,
just as whatever rivers there may be flow toward the great ocean.
"Thus may the worlds, including the devas,
come into your presence.
Thus praised and extolled by them, he—
Having undertaken ten qualities,
fulfilling those qualities,
he then entered the forest.
The Discourse on the Resolve of Sumedha is concluded.
